content: Prontosil was a groundbreaking discovery in the field of medicine, marking the advent of sulfonamide drugs. It was developed by the German chemical conglomerate IG Farben. The compound, sulfonamidochrysoidine (also known as KI-730), was first synthesized by Bayer chemists Josef Klarer and Fritz Mietzsch. Its antibacterial properties were demonstrated in mice by Gerhard Domagk, who later received the 1939 Nobel Prize in Medicine for this work. The development of Prontosil was the result of five years of intensive research and testing, involving thousands of compounds related to azo dyes. The pivotal experiment that established its antibacterial efficacy in a murine model of systemic Streptococcus pyogenes infection was conducted in late December 1931. The sodium salt of sulfonamidochrysoidine, which is water-soluble and produces a burgundy red solution, was trademarked as Prontosil. Clinical investigations of Prontosil were carried out between 1932 and 1934, initially at the Wuppertal-Elberfeld hospital under Philipp Klee and later at the Düsseldorf University Hospital. The clinical results were published in a series of articles in the February 15, 1935, issue of the prestigious German medical journal Deutsche Medizinische Wochenschrift. Initially, the medical community, which was focused on vaccination and crude immunotherapy, received these findings with skepticism. However, as reports of Prontosil's clinical successes began to emerge from across Europe, and especially after its widely publicized use in treating Franklin Delano Roosevelt Jr. (the son of U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt), acceptance grew rapidly. This spurred numerous medicinal chemistry teams to work on improving Prontosil. In 1936, Jacques and Thérèse Tréfouël and their team at the French Pasteur Institute discovered that Prontosil is metabolized in the body to sulfanilamide (para-aminophenylsulfonamide), a simpler and colorless molecule. This redefined Prontosil as a prodrug. Sulfanilamide, which had been synthesized as early as 1909 by Paul Gelmo during his doctoral research at the University of Vienna, was off-patent and inexpensive to produce. Its structure also allowed for easy chemical modification, leading to the development of hundreds of second-generation sulfonamide drugs. Despite its initial success, Prontosil did not generate the profits Bayer had hoped for, as it was quickly overshadowed by these newer sulfa drugs. By the mid-1940s and 1950s, the introduction of penicillin and other antibiotics, which were more effective against a broader range of bacterial infections, further diminished its use. Nevertheless, Prontosil remained on the market until the 1960s. The discovery of Prontosil had a profound impact on the history of medicine, ushering in the antibiotic era and revolutionizing pharmaceutical research, drug regulations, and medical treatment. Even today, sulfonamide-trimethoprim combinations are used for treating opportunistic infections in AIDS patients, urinary tract infections, and burn therapy, although their use has largely been supplanted by beta-lactam antibiotics.
